power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < .05", "p < .05", "p < .05"), Text = c("Here, we only show the variables that had a significant change in correlation coefficient after controlling for multiple comparisons (p < .05).", "The beta was still significant (p < .05), but smaller.", "When including household income satisfaction, this beta coefficient, or difference between old and young Norwegians in absolute terms, shrank to .34 (p < .001) and reduced to .25 (p < .05) when including the Affect Balance factor as well." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .151", Sentence = "In M1 (Table S1 p = .151) but moved toward zero afterwards (0.0059 per year, p p = .004)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: In most of the world's countries, young adults report the highest well-being among different age groups.
A notable exception has emerged in North America and Northern Europe, where this pattern has reversed, with older adults reporting greater well-being than the young.

We analyzed Gallup World Poll data from 2006-2025, covering 2.9 million respondents worldwide and 17,007 in Norway, to examine shifts in the age gap in well-being (as measured with the life evaluation metric, the Cantril Ladder) and possible determinants.

Norway is a particularly valuable case for illustrating this reversal since the country ranked as the world's happiest in 2017, but has declined in both absolute terms and relative rankings, with national statistics revealing a pronounced wellbeing gap between young and old.

We found that the decline in life evaluation scores in Norway largely reflects lower scores among young adults (<30 years), whose scores have dropped significantly since 2017 (p < .001; d = 0.36) and are now markedly lower than those of older adults (60+; p < .001; d = 0.34).
text.formatted: We found that the decline in life evaluation scores in Norway largely reflects lower scores among young adults (<30 years), whose scores have dropped significantly since 2017 (p < .001; d = 0.36) and are now markedly lower than those of older adults (60+; p < .001; d = 0.34).

text.text: We further confirmed that this trend is limited to a small set of countries.
Of all 2,648 correlations between age and life evaluation across 159 different countries and 20 years, 83% were negative, and only 3% exceeded .10, the magnitude observed in Norway 2023-2025.
We examined potential explanations of the observed change in Norway.

Only a few of the 50 candidate variables in the Gallup World Poll were found to be related to the increased age difference in life evaluations in Norway; the most important variables were i) affect-related factors (e.g., feeling well-rested and sadness), and ii) socioeconomic satisfaction (e.g., satisfaction with standard of living and household income, although not absolute income) iii) institutional trust (e.g., confidence in the government and judicial system).
This study emphasizes the imperative for highly developed countries to prioritise the well-being of their young despite overall prosperity and high living standards.
Who is happier, the young or the old?

Findings on the association between age and wellbeing are mixed and range from no relationship to positive and negative age gradients, as well as reports of U-curves and J-curves (Bartram, 2021 (Bartram, , 2023;; Blanchflower et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2022; Helliwell et al., 2024).

text.text: Recent studies suggest a decline in well-being among the young, in some countries and regions (Helliwell et al., 2024).

text.text: However, there is limited knowledge about the relations between age and well-being worldwide, how these relations have changed over time, and the factors driving such changes.
Here, we use Norway as a case for studying age differences in life evaluations.
In 2017 Norway was ranked as the world's happiest country (Helliwell et al., 2017) but has since fallen to the lowest level of life evaluation among the Nordic countries (Helliwell et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In 2017 Norway was ranked as the world's happiest country <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Helliwell et al., 2017)</ref> but has since fallen to the lowest level of life evaluation among the Nordic countries <ref type="bibr">(Helliwell et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Which processes and factors have been involved in this development from summit to slope?

We set out to examine whether Norway's relative decline in life evaluations is due to a particular decline among the young, when it happened, to what extent the developments in Norway are paralleled in other countries, and which factors may explain the recent trends.
Life evaluation refers to a person's reflective assessment of their life as a whole, rather than to a specific component of well-being such as positive affect, meaning, or functioning.
It is typically measured using the Cantril Ladder, which asks respondents to place their lives on a ladder ranging from the worst possible life for them to the best possible life for them.
The measure therefore captures a broad, global evaluation of one's life, but does not by itself provide a comprehensive assessment of well-being or its constituent dimensions.
The Cantril Ladder is the primary metric reported in the World Happiness Report (WHR; Helliwell et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The Cantril Ladder is the primary metric reported in the World Happiness Report (WHR; <ref type="bibr">Helliwell et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, its framing may lead respondents to think about power and wealth rather than broader well-being (Nilsson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, its framing may lead respondents to think about power and wealth rather than broader well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Nilsson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It nevertheless remains widely used for global comparisons and shows strong empirical overlap with life satisfaction, especially in highly developed countries (Bjørnskov, 2010).
text.formatted: It nevertheless remains widely used for global comparisons and shows strong empirical overlap with life satisfaction, especially in highly developed countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bjørnskov, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Several studies have reported a U-shaped relationship between age and well-being, with lower well-being among middle-aged adults than among younger and older adults (cf. Blanchflower, 2021; Helliwell et al., 2024).

text.text: This finding has been criticized on methodological grounds, particularly for relying on analyses that include potentially inappropriate control variables (Bartram, 2021 (Bartram, , 2023;; Glenn, 2009; Hellevik, 2017).

text.text: Even when these methodological concerns are taken into account, young people have generally reported high levels of well-being, for example in Norway (Hellevik, 2017), while older adults have reported levels of well-being comparable to, or even higher than, those of younger adults, despite age-related declines in physical health, functional capacity, and social resources (the well-being paradox of aging; Baltes & Baltes, 1990; Blanchflower & Oswald, 2008).

text.text: However, recent evidence paints an increasingly complex picture of how life evaluations vary with age and cohorts (Helliwell et al., 2024).

text.text: In some regions, the U-shaped pattern seems to have shifted to a linear, or nearly linear, negative association, with younger adults reporting higher life evaluations than older ones (cf. Blanchflower et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2022; Helliwell et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In some regions, the U-shaped pattern seems to have shifted to a linear, or nearly linear, negative association, with younger adults reporting higher life evaluations than older ones (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Blanchflower et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Chen et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Helliwell et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Other studies indicate a J-shaped pattern, with almost flat levels across young adulthood and midlife (with only slightly lower levels in midlife) while older adults show substantially higher levels (cf. Lomas et al., 2025).

text.text: In contrast, in North America and Norway, younger adults report lower life evaluation than older adults, producing a positive linear association between age and life evaluation (Chen et al., 2022; Helliwell et al., 2024).

text.text: The 2024 WHR underscores this rare reversal, showing that people under 30 reported the lowest life evaluation in 7 of 143 countries (Helliwell et al., 2024).

text.text: Additionally, when ranking countries by changes in life evaluation among those under 25, the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand (the NANZ region) fall near the bottom, placing them between 122nd and 133rd out of 136 countries (Helliwell et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Additionally, when ranking countries by changes in life evaluation among those under 25, the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand (the NANZ region) fall near the bottom, placing them between 122nd and 133rd out of 136 countries <ref type="bibr">(Helliwell et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This indicates that young people in these countries have experienced some of the largest declines in life evaluation globally during the past years.
The onset and development of this shift, along with its underlying causes, remain unclear, sparking growing concern and debate about the well-being of young people.
These patterns, however, are largely based on cross-sectional data, which conflate age, period, and cohort effects, a limitation that applies equally to the life evaluation findings reported above.

Longitudinal evidence, by contrast, indicates that life satisfaction typically increases modestly but systematically from around age 16 into the 60s and then declines in late old age (Buecker et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Longitudinal evidence, by contrast, indicates that life satisfaction typically increases modestly but systematically from around age 16 into the 60s and then declines in late old age <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Buecker et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In sum, age differences may reflect both normative developmental change and cohortor period-specific influences.
Notably, Buecker et al.'s study found no evidence that birth cohort (year of birth) moderated the slopes of change in life satisfaction, positive affect, or negative affect.

Their database, however, is dominated by high-income, predominantly Western samples, and does not support strong conclusions about cohort differences in mean levels of well-being or recent sociohistorical shifts in younger generations' well-being (cf. Gerstorf et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Their database, however, is dominated by high-income, predominantly Western samples, and does not support strong conclusions about cohort differences in mean levels of well-being or recent sociohistorical shifts in younger generations' well-being (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Gerstorf et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Further insights into this phenomenon are crucial both for advancing theories and understanding of the factors that shape population well-being, and for informing effective policy responses, which would require broader global data.
Norway represents a particularly interesting case for understanding young life evaluation and its change.
It has a reputation as one of the world's happiest countries and topped the global rankings in 2017 (Helliwell et al., 2017).
text.formatted: It has a reputation as one of the world's happiest countries and topped the global rankings in 2017 <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Helliwell et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Less than a decade later, however, the picture looks different: while point estimates of life evaluation have risen across the other Nordic countries, Norway has declined by 0.30 points and now ranks as the least happy among them (Helliwell et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Less than a decade later, however, the picture looks different: while point estimates of life evaluation have risen across the other Nordic countries, Norway has declined by 0.30 points and now ranks as the least happy among them <ref type="bibr">(Helliwell et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, there are signs that young people fare worse than older adults.

Recent studies indicate that Norwegian adolescents and young adults score lower on life evaluation and mental health than the rest of the adult population (Hellevik & Hellevik, 2021; Kozák et al., 2023; Nes & Ørstavik, 2022; Potrebny et al., 2019; Potrebny et al., 2025).

text.text: In fact, a near-linear positive association with age has been observed for life evaluation and related wellbeing measures (e.g., meaning in life, positive emotions, trust) since 2019-2020, when comprehensive monitoring of national and regional well-being was introduced in Norway (Aarø et al., 2024).

text.text: This pattern is striking because Norway is a wealthy welfare state with strong social institutions, and relative economic resilience which might be expected to buffer younger adults from economic pressures.
Nevertheless, young people in Norway, as in other high-income countries, face a range of challenges.
They navigate complex transitions through education and employment under increasing pressure from housing affordability and living costs (Cournède & Plouin, 2022; Eurofound, 2024; OECD, 2022, 2025).
text.formatted: They navigate complex transitions through education and employment under increasing pressure from housing affordability and living costs (Cournède & Plouin, 2022; Eurofound, 2024; OECD, 2022, 2025).

text.text: The transition to parenthood is occurring later than in previous cohorts (OECD, 2022), alongside changes in fertility intentions and expectations about family formation (Dommermuth et al., 2025), which may reflect a change in the content and timing of normative life scripts rather than their disappearance (Janssen & Rubin, 2011; Liefbroer & Billari, 2010).

text.text: Digitalisation has also reshaped how young people communicate, work, and form and maintain relationships (OECD, 2019; Nesi et al., 2018).
Taken together, these contrasting factors make Norway an informative context for examining age differences in life evaluation over time.

When the age gradient in life evaluations shifted, the extent to which declining life evaluations among young adults contributed to the overall decline, whether similar shifts are evident in other countries, and what factors underlie these developments remain unclear.
Several candidate mechanisms have been proposed.
The most widely discussed is perhaps social media use, but findings remain mixed.

Meta-analytic, cross-national, and longitudinal evidence indicates that relations between social media use and reduced life evaluations tend to be small but heterogeneous (Helliwell et al., 2026; Huang, 2022; Orben & Przybylski, 2019; Twenge et al., 2020), although some scholars argue that the effects are larger than these syntheses indicate (Haidt & Allen, 2020).

text.text: Another explanation, particularly relevant in Norway, may be a growing gap in financial stability between younger and older adults (Normann,  In the present study, we examine changes in life evaluation across age groups in Norway between 2006 and 2025.

text.text: Specifically, we pursue three main objectives.
First, we aim to identify when the age gradient in life evaluation shifted in Norway.
Second, we seek to place the Norwegian findings in an international context by examining whether similar age-related patterns in life evaluation can be observed in other countries.
Finally, we aim to explore potential factors underlying the observed trend in Norway.
We capitalized on the Gallup World Poll (GWP), a global survey designed to measure public opinion and monitor key wellbeing indicators across countries (Gallup, 2011; 2019).
text.formatted: We capitalized on the Gallup World Poll (GWP), a global survey designed to measure public opinion and monitor key wellbeing indicators across countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Gallup, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2019)</ref>.

text.text: It involves nationally representative samples of the adult population aged 15 and older, with approximately 1,000 people per country annually, with a different selection of people each year.
The GWP survey usually takes 15-20 minutes to complete, and includes around 60-80 questions (the number varies across respondents based on screener items, filters and skip patterns).
This paper is based on data spanning all years of the GWP from 2006 to 2025 with the Norwegian data lacking in 2007, 2009-2011 and 2013.
There were a total of 3,012,810 participants in the sample.

After excluding respondents with less than $100 in annual household income and respondents with no data on Cantril Ladder, age and gender, 2,933,981 participants remained, of which 17,007 were in Norway.
Data collection was undertaken in accordance with the established protocol of the GWP.
Data collection in Norway was conducted by phone every year.
We used listwise deletion for missing data, given that missing values were rare.
The 71 variables (67 candidate variables plus life evaluation, age, gender, and weights) used in the analysis comprised 893 variable-by-year measurements.
The mean missingness, defined as responses of either "I don't know" or "refused to answer", was 1.73%, with a median of 0.5% (maximum 28%), across the 893 variable-by-year measurements.
We adopted the age groups used in the WHR special chapter (Helliwell et al., 2024): below 30 years, 30-60 years, and 60+ years (the distribution of these age groups can be seen in Figure S16).
text.formatted: We adopted the age groups used in the WHR special chapter <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Helliwell et al., 2024</ref>): below 30 years, 30-60 years, and 60+ years (the distribution of these age groups can be seen in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">S16</ref>).

text.text: In the WHR, the middle-aged group was further divided into 30-45 and 46-60, but in the case of Norway this finer division made little difference (Supplemental Figure S5), and we hence retained three groups for clarity in the main manuscript.
text.formatted: In the WHR, the middle-aged group was further divided into 30-45 and 46-60, but in the case of Norway this finer division made little difference (Supplemental Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_11">S5</ref>), and we hence retained three groups for clarity in the main manuscript.

text.text: Although the age group distribution was imbalanced, with 15% of the data in the below 30 age group and 50% in the middle-aged group, Gallup has sampling weights for age, gender and socioeconomic status; hence, we chose to keep the three age groups despite the imbalance for ease of interpretation.
We further ran analyses treating age both as a categorical (grouped) variable and as a continuous variable.
Defining age groups by current age rather than birth cohort implies that group composition changes over time.
For example, the sub 30 age group was born 1976-1991 in the 2006 assessment, but 1995-2010 in the 2025 assessment.
Cohort-based analyses are shown in Supplemental Material Figure S1.
text.formatted: Cohort-based analyses are shown in Supplemental Material Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">S1</ref>.

text.text: The main item of interest was the life evaluation question in the GWP, the Cantril Ladder (Cantril, 1965), which is phrased as follows: "Please imagine a ladder, with steps numbered from 0 at the bottom to 10 at the top.
text.formatted: The main item of interest was the life evaluation question in the GWP, the Cantril Ladder <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cantril, 1965)</ref>, which is phrased as follows: "Please imagine a ladder, with steps numbered from 0 at the bottom to 10 at the top.

text.text: The top of the ladder represents the best possible life for you and the bottom of the ladder represents the worst possible life for you.
On which step of the ladder would you say you personally feel you stand at this time?"
In most of our analyses, we used the Cantril Ladder as the WHR does, meaning that we took the average of the last three years to offer clean comparisons.
The WHR also uses threeyear averages to increase statistical power -a rationale that is relevant in our study too, particularly when examining subgroups.
We present yearly assessments in the Supplemental Material Figure S6.
text.formatted: We present yearly assessments in the Supplemental Material Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_12">S6</ref>.

text.text: We explored 67 other candidate variables in the GWP as potential explanatory factors of the strengthening association between age and life evaluation in Norway (see Table S4).
text.formatted: We explored 67 other candidate variables in the GWP as potential explanatory factors of the strengthening association between age and life evaluation in Norway (see Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: These ranged from affective experiences (e.g., experienced enjoyment the previous day), to economic standards (e.g., actual household income and satisfaction with household income), to institutional trust (e.g., corruption in business and government) and safety (e.g., feeling safe walking at night) measures.
Of note, some GWP items were only asked in a few years (e.g., liking what you do every day).
We used all variables that were measured at least two years in or before 2017 and that were also measured at least two years in 2018 or later.
Hence, we made use of all available Gallup variables with enough data before and after 2017.
To reduce the 67 candidate variables to broader domains and reduce the number of statistical tests, we conducted a principal component analysis with oblimin rotation.

To prevent specific years from shaping the structure, each variable was standardised within each survey year, and the analysis was run on the pairwise correlation matrix pooled across 2006-2025, so that no respondents were excluded for missing items.
The scree plot levelled off after six components, which together explained 25% of the variance.
Of these six, we selected three based on interpretability and stability.

The components were Institutional Trust (10 items, e.g., confidence in the national government and the judicial system), Affect Balance (5 items: enjoyment, smiling, feeling well-rested, [low] worry and [low] sadness), and City Likeability (5 items, e.g., city satisfaction and the city being a good place for immigrants).
Component scores were the mean of the salient items (loading .40), ≥ standardised across all years so that change over time was preserved.
To assess stability, we refitted the solution separately in 2015-2017 and 2023-2025 and compared the loadings with Tucker's congruence coefficient.
Across periods, congruence for the three components was .94, .74 and .85 over all loadings, and .99, .89 and .99 over the items defining each component.
Affect Balance was the least stable because smiling and enjoyment loaded more weakly in 2015-2017.
The remaining 47 items that did not make it into any of the factors were entered as single variables.
Scree plot, loadings and stability statistics are reported in Table S3 and Figures S10-11.
text.formatted: Scree plot, loadings and stability statistics are reported in Table <ref type="table">S3</ref> and Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_16">S10-11</ref>.

text.text: The analysis focused primarily on the trajectory of life evaluation across age and time in Norway.
When comparing different periods, we specifically examined the years 2015-2017 against 2023-2025.

Norway ranked number 1 in the world in 2017 with an average life evaluation of 7.537 (data spanning 2014-2016) but was beaten by Finland (and Norway ranked number 2) in 2018 with data from 2015-2017 despite an increase in absolute average to 7.594.
We thus compared Norway's 2015-2017 life evaluation peak with the most recent three-year period, i.e., 2023-2025.
We first examined life evaluation trends for the three age groups i) below 30, ii) 30-60, and iii) 60+, between 2006 and 2025.
To do this, we grouped survey responses into overlapping three-year periods (e.g., 2023-2025 representing 2025) and assigned each participant to the period in which they were interviewed.
We then fitted a weighted linear regression predicting the Cantril Ladder score from year, age group, their interaction, and gender.

From this model we extracted adjusted mean scores for each age group in each period, and calculated Cohen's d to quantify (1) how much each age group's mean changed from one period to the next, and (2) how large the gap was between age groups within each period.
Finally, these adjusted means were plotted with smoothed trend lines.
Next, we examined developments in the life evaluation-age association across all countries.

We applied weighted correlations in each country and year across the GWP dataset between 2006 and 2025; here, we did not average life evaluation across the last three years, to get independent correlations.
This resulted in 2,648 unique correlations.
We plotted the correlations against year with one smoothed trend line per country (n = 159).
To highlight countries where older people have come to evaluate their life higher than young people (in a linear fashion), we chose two inclusion criteria.
First, the correlation in 2023-2025 had to be at least .10 stronger than the correlation in 2015-2017.
Second, the correlation in 2023-2025 had to be r ≥ .10 to align with at least small-sized positive correlation coefficients (Gignac and Szodorai, 2016).

text.text: To confirm the patterns in the global correlation analysis, we estimated multilevel models that made use of all the data.
These were linear mixed models with respondents nested in country-years within countries, and a crossed random intercept for survey year.
We regressed life evaluation on standardised age and survey year.
Year was entered as two linear slopes joined at 2017, the year Norway ranked first in the World Happiness Report.
Age × year interactions captured whether the association between age and life evaluation changed before and after 2017.
We allowed the age slope and its interactions with year to vary across countries, and the age slope to vary across country-years.
A second model added age² and its interactions with year.
From the first model, we derived each country's age gradient (fixed effects plus country random effects) with 95% intervals, averaged over the windows used in Figure 2.

text.text: The final group of analyses aimed to explain the emerging difference in life evaluation change across age in Norway.
We first looked at how much each of the variables (47 single items and three factors) increased in explained variance in a multiple regression with age and year for two different time periods.
This analysis screened for variables that became more strongly associated with life evaluation as the age gap in life evaluation grew.
We ran a multiple regression using the formula life evaluation ~ year + age + candidate variable.
This analysis was performed for two time periods, 2006 to 2017 and 2018 to 2025.
Our goal was to identify which candidate variable resulted in the largest adjusted R² increase.
We established three cutoff years, 2015, 2016, and 2017, to enhance the robustness of the analysis and make sure no single year disproportionately influenced the results.
We focused on the average of the adjusted R² differences.
The results from the analysis showed how much additional variance each candidate variable explained in life evaluation next to age and time between the early and late time periods.
A large difference indicates that the candidate variable explained more variance in the recent time period than in the earlier time period.
Second, we looked at the strength of the weighted correlation coefficient between life evaluation and each candidate variable among those under 30, comparing 2015-2017 and 2023-2025.
We significance-tested the correlation strength differences and plotted those that were significantly stronger in 2023-2025 compared to 2015-2017.
To test whether the association between each candidate variable and life evaluation changed over time, we additionally estimated variable × year interactions among the below 30 age group.
Life evaluation and each candidate variable were z-standardised using weighted means and standard deviations, and all models were estimated with the Gallup sample weights.

For each variable we fitted two models of the change in association: (i) a linear trend across the full series (variable × year); (ii) a piecewise trend allowing an additional change in slope after 2017, the year of the break in the age-life evaluation association.
Because many variables were tested, we controlled for multiple comparisons with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure within each model type.
Third, we looked at the standardised mean difference (i.e., the difference in zstandardised group means) between the below 30 and above 60 age groups in the two different time periods.
We compared the difference in 2015-2017 and 2023-2025 and plotted the 10 variables with the strongest change.

Finally, we evaluated the mediating effect of the candidate variables on the age-life evaluation relationship in 2023-2025, comparing the standardised beta of age on life evaluation when it was the sole predictor and how much the standardised beta of age shrank after adding each of the candidate variables.

Since age cannot be caused by any psychological variables, we can assess the mediation on the age-life evaluation relationship simply by examining how much the relationship decreases when adding each candidate variable.
This interpretation assumes that life evaluation does not cause the candidate variables and that they share no common causes, which cross-sectional data cannot establish.
We present the mediating effect of the two candidate variables that had the strongest mediating effect.

Based on the results of the above analyses, we presented the piecewise linear trends before and after 2017 of the variables that showed the strongest indications of being involved in the change of the life evaluation-age association.

Amid growing international concern about the well-being of young people (Handa et al., 2023; Marquez et al., 2024) and recent shifts in the age distribution of well-being (Blanchflower et al., 2025; Twenge & Blanchflower, 2025), the present study set out to address three interrelated research questions using data from 2.9 million individuals across the world and 17,000 respondents in Norway, over 20 years.
text.formatted: Amid growing international concern about the well-being of young people <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Handa et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Marquez et al., 2024)</ref> and recent shifts in the age distribution of well-being (Blanchflower et al., 2025; Twenge & Blanchflower, 2025), the present study set out to address three interrelated research questions using data from 2.9 million individuals across the world and 17,000 respondents in Norway, over 20 years.

text.text: Our first research question concerned when the age gradient in well-being changed in Norway.
We found that this shift occurred around 2017, after which young Norwegians reported lower life evaluation than their older 60+ counterparts.
Our second research question placed the Norwegian findings in an international context by examining whether similar age-well-being patterns were evident in other countries.
Only a few countries, predominantly Nordic and English-speaking, showed a pattern similar to that observed in Norway.
Finally, our third research question investigated factors that may underlie this trend in Norway.
We found some support for subjective economic standards, emotional health, and institutional trust factors as potential explanations.
Our findings document a historically recent change in the distribution of life evaluations across age groups in Norway.

The findings are in line with observations based on The Norwegian Public Health Surveys (Aarø et al., 2024), which consistently report lower well-being among the young and a near-linear gradient across age groups, since they started collecting data in 2019.

text.text: Data from the Ipsos Norwegian Monitor, ranging back to 1985, show a marked decline in happiness and life satisfaction ratings among the young samples (15-39 years) between 2009 and 2019, contrasting an earlier period (1985-2009) characterized by stable or modestly rising levels (Hellevik & Hellevik, 2021).

text.text: This latter study also suggests that the downward trend among the young samples accounts for the observed negative trajectory at the Norwegian population level.
Declines in mental health and increases in loneliness have also been reported among Norwegian adolescent samples (von Soest et al., 2022; Kozák et al., 2023).

text.text: Our analyses show that the age pattern observed in Norway is only evident in a few other countries such as Sweden, China, Canada, and the US.
These findings are in line with studies using other data sets than the GWP, which also indicate a shifting age trend in such countries (Chen et al., 2022; Twenge & Blanchflower, 2025).
text.formatted: These findings are in line with studies using other data sets than the GWP, which also indicate a shifting age trend in such countries (Chen et al., 2022; Twenge & Blanchflower, 2025).

text.text: Because these countries differ in welfare provision and affluence, the Norwegian decline is unlikely to be explained solely by factors unique to Norway.
A corresponding pattern is also evident for mental ill-being (e.g., anxiety and depressive symptoms).

Pooled cross-sectional Global Minds data across 44 countries from 2020-2025, including the US and the United Kingdom (UK), show that scores on five different indicators of mental ill-being are higher among younger respondents than among older ones (Blanchflower et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Pooled cross-sectional Global Minds data across 44 countries from 2020-2025, including the US and the United Kingdom (UK), show that scores on five different indicators of mental ill-being are higher among younger respondents than among older ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Blanchflower et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In both the US and the UK, this shift appears to have begun before the pandemic, which accelerated an existing trajectory.
Notably, these age comparisons are cross-sectional and therefore cannot establish whether the observed differences reflect agerelated changes or birth cohort differences.
Nor can they fully disentangle age, cohort, and period effects.
Several contextual features make Norway an informative case for understanding shifts in young adults' well-being.
The country combines high average life evaluations (Statistics Norway, 2025b) with extensive welfare protection and comparatively low levels of material deprivation (OECD, 2025).

Yet young adults face rising housing costs (OECD, 2022), growing social gradients (Goldblatt et al., 2023), rapid technological change requiring continuous reskilling (Fauske, 2020), and societal pressures relating to climate concerns (Hickman et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Yet young adults face rising housing costs (OECD, 2022), growing social gradients <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Goldblatt et al., 2023)</ref>, rapid technological change requiring continuous reskilling (Fauske, 2020), and societal pressures relating to climate concerns <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Hickman et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Most of these pressures are shared with other high-income countries, which fits the similar age patterns we observed in, for example, Sweden, Canada, and the United States.
Together they may help explain why the well-being of young Norwegians has declined despite the buffers a wealthy welfare state would be expected to provide.
Our findings point to three clusters of explanatory factors, which echo these broader pressures.
The first is economic and material living conditions.
The identified economic risk factors include dissatisfaction with household income and living standards, but not reported income.

More than twice as many younger Norwegians (13%) were dissatisfied with their household income compared with older adults (5%) in 2023-2025 and this difference appeared to account for part of the difference in life evaluation scores.

Given the subjective nature of the household income satisfaction item, the economic connotations of the Cantril Ladder (Nilsson et al., 2024), and the association between income and well-being (e.g., Killingsworth et al., 2023), it is not surprising that the two variables share some variance.

text.text: Wealth among Norwegians aged 60+ has increased markedly, and older adults have benefited from income growth and labour participation, drawing on both pensions and earnings (Normann, 2022; Hattrem, 2022).

text.text: Consistent with our GWP findings, the national wellbeing surveys 2020-2025 show that 50% of adults under 25 report financial dissatisfaction compared with one third of those aged 45-66, and fewer than 20% of those aged 66 and older (Statistics Norway, 2025c).

A national student survey likewise found high rates of financial difficulties, linked to elevated risks of mental health problems, self-harm, suicide attempts, failed exams (Bøe et al., 2021), and major depression at one-year follow-up (Sivertsen et al., 2025).

text.text: The second cluster concerns emotional health.
Affective experiences became more closely tied to life evaluation among the young.

Adding the Affect Balance factor to the model with age and life evaluation reduced the age coefficient by 43%, and anger showed the largest shift in association with life evaluation among Norwegians under 30, followed by pain.
Anger levels themselves did not increase significantly over the period, but what changed was how closely anger experiences were tied to life evaluations.

In general, the rise in emotional health problems among the young is consistent with other findings on the matter, in Norway as well as globally (Almeida et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2022; Thapar et al., 2022).

text.text: Third, the trend in Institutional Trust reversed.
In 2015-2017, young Norwegians scored higher than older ones on Institutional Trust; by 2023-2025, older Norwegians scored higher.
Institutional trust is often seen as an explanation for why the Nordic countries score high on life evaluation (Martela et al., 2020).

text.text: Although younger Norwegian adults continue to report life evaluation ratings above the global average, the observed negative trend among this group is concerning.

Our findings indicate a decline in life evaluation ratings among Norwegian young adults (i.e., <30), and the difference is statistically significant, with a Cohen's d of 0.34 relative to those aged 60 and above in 2025.

text.text: This effect size is small to medium in absolute terms, but it is concerning because it did not exist some years ago.
This trend raises important societal concerns.
Sustained decline in young people's wellbeing may impair the functioning of future generations, with potential consequences for social and economic productivity and national flourishing.

text.text: In long-lived societies such as Norway, younger adults may adjust their expectations to support sustained investment in education, career, and personal growth over a longer life course, particularly given that the life evaluation metric (the Cantril Ladder) is related to social status, hierarchy, and wealth (Nilsson et al., 2024).

text.text: Such recalibration can be adaptive, promoting long-term planning and growth.

Taken together, the observed age differences in life evaluation likely reflect a combination of adaptive developmental processes, societal context, and potential risk factors, highlighting the importance of monitoring trends while considering their nuanced interpretation.
Our analyses were based on a large data set spanning 20 years.
The observed trends and age group differences are robust and statistically significant, although small to medium in size.
However, when it comes to explanatory factors, our analyses are exploratory and cannot provide evidence of causality.
Rather, these factors should be considered candidates for further exploration and testing.

This is particularly important because the present analysis adopted a data-driven approach, after initially testing whether changes in stress, income, and social support explained the change based on theoretical assumptions, but found little evidence that they did.
In addition, some conceptual overlap may exist between several of the affective candidate variables and life evaluation, as both capture aspects of well-being.

The direction of the associations is also uncertain: a stronger association between, for example, anger and life evaluation could mean that life evaluation shapes how anger is reported, or that a third factor affects both.
Notably, in some analyses, access to a landline phone and internet access emerged as explanatory variables.
Although these variables most likely reflect broader technological changes, their appearance provides face validity for the analysis by capturing trends that would be expected to appear in the data.
Further, additional factors not captured by our dataset may contribute to the decline in life evaluation among Norwegians under 30.
These could include country-specific characteristics, such as economic conditions, social policies, cultural norms, or welfare systems.

While cohort patterns are shown descriptively (see Supplemental Figure S1), our study primarily examines age differences over time, and explicitly disentangling age, period, and cohort effects is beyond the scope of this analysis.

text.text: Changes in the demographic composition of the population could in principle contribute to the age differences we observe.

Immigration to Norway increased after the Russian invasion of Ukraine (Statistics Norway, 2026), and in the Gallup data the share of participants under 30 born abroad rose from 2020, more steeply than among those aged 60 and above.
Those under 30 born abroad reported lower life evaluations than those born in Norway, but only in 2024.
Three considerations argue against immigration as a major explanation.

The Gallup data do not specify respondents' countries of origin; the difference appeared in only one survey year; and recent studies from Sweden show that being foreign-born is associated with little or no difference in well-being (Bittár et al., 2025; Nilsson et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The Gallup data do not specify respondents' countries of origin; the difference appeared in only one survey year; and recent studies from Sweden show that being foreign-born is associated with little or no difference in well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bittár et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Nilsson et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Demographic change may nevertheless contribute to shifts in the age-life evaluation association and warrants further investigation in data with more detailed information on migration background.

Furthermore, individuals entering young adulthood around 2017 -coinciding with the onset of the well-being decline among young populations -were the first generation to have spent their entire teenage years with social media and smartphones.

Previous studies have linked social media use to lower well-being, particularly when it involves social comparison (e.g., Marciano et al., 2024), and increased social comparison may plausibly reduce perceived financial well-being -a factor consistently associated with higher life satisfaction (e.g., Ngamaba et al., 2020; She et al., 2021).

text.text: We could not examine social media use directly, as the GWP does not include questions on social media use or social comparison.
Future studies incorporating these variables could help clarify additional mechanisms underpinning the observed decline.
Moreover, our findings should be interpreted considering the analytical procedures employed.
Specifically, we did some analyses by dividing the data into subgroups, which affected the effective sample size.
However, analyses treating age as continuous, thus increasing statistical power, yielded similar results.
Additionally, the use of probability-based sampling and the inclusion of weights enhance the robustness and representativeness of our results.
Another limitation of our study is that several of the items used as predictors were relatively narrow in scope, and the binary response scales restricted our ability to detect nuanced variability.
Finally, our assessment of well-being relied on a single life evaluation item, the Cantril Ladder.

Scholars have argued that focusing solely on life evaluations provides an incomplete picture of well-being and advocate for a more comprehensive, multidimensional approach (Marsh et al., 2020; Martela & Ryan, 2023; OECD, 2013).
text.formatted: Scholars have argued that focusing solely on life evaluations provides an incomplete picture of well-being and advocate for a more comprehensive, multidimensional approach (Marsh et al., 2020; Martela & Ryan, 2023; OECD, 2013).

text.text: Thus, future research should incorporate multidimensional indicators of well-being to gain a more comprehensive understanding of how well-being among young individuals has changed over time.
In 2017, Norway was ranked as the happiest country in the world.
Since then, average life evaluations have declined, and by 2026 Norway ranked lowest among the Nordic countries.
Our analyses suggest that the decline is concentrated among adults under 60 and is steepest among young adults, while older adults continue to report relatively high scores.

The current Norwegian pattern, in which older adults report higher life evaluations than younger adults and life evaluation is almost linearly positively associated with age, also appears in a few other countries, most notably Sweden, Canada, the United States and China.
Finally, age differences in economic satisfaction, emotional health, and institutional trust emerge as potential explanatory factors in Norway.

We encourage future research to devote greater attention to understanding both the decrease in young adults' life evaluations and the sustained high life evaluation in older adults, in Norway as well as in other countries where the young's life evaluations appear to be declining.

text.text: Young was operationalised as sub 30 vs 60+ of age to get a distinct comparison.

We also tested a Difference-in-difference (DiD) approach where we predicted life evaluation from age group, a post-2017 indicator and their interaction (the DiD term) plus 46 mediators and their interaction with the DiD term.

This was seen as the most appropriate model analysis to understand the increasing life evaluation-age gap, as the analysis determines whether a change in difference in one candidate variable follows the change in life evaluation between age groups.

We first excluded any mediator with more than 25 % missing data, reducing the number of candidate variables to 46, then limited the sample to participants under 30 ("young") or 60 and over ("old") to get the strongest difference.
Life evaluation scores were standardized and combined with a post-2017 indicator and their product formed the DiD term.
Remaining mediators were standardised, and a model with age, period, mediators, and mediator×DID interactions as predictors was constructed.

A survey-weighted, 10-fold cross-validated LASSO regression then identified which mediator×DID terms retained nonzero coefficients at the optimal penalty -those variables whose link to well-being shifted most between young and old after 2017.
As the interaction terms were the ones of interest, we only penalised the interactions, to avoid main effects pushing the interaction terms' effects to 0.
To make the analysis more robust, we did three models where we shifted the post-2017 indicator to be post-2016 in one model and post-2015 in another model, and then averaging the beta coefficients.

As the DiD approach was relatively complex and did not provide clear results, we focus more on the three other analyses that were simpler and may help in understanding the change in the life evaluation-age association.
The Affect Balance factor variable had a negative beta, indicating that its relationship with life evaluation decreased more for young than older Norwegians.
Looking at the correlations to life evaluation for Norwegian young adults, confidence in elections was related at r = .26 in 2015-2017 but increased to r = .40 in 2023-2025.
For older Norwegians, the relationship increased from r = .41 in 2015-2017 to r = .43 in 2022-2024.

Thus, the Affect Balance factor became more important for Norwegians below 30 compared to older Norwegian people and as the younger population decreased in absolute scores, the variable may explain a small portion of the emerging age-life evaluation gap.
In a developed country like Norway, the landline phone access effect might reflect the severe drop in landline phones among older people.
In 2015-2017, 60% of Norwegians above 60 had landline phones, which dropped to 6% in 2023-2025.
For Norwegians below 30, the drop was from 16% in 2015-2017 to 9% in 2023-2025.
Thus, the change in difference between old and young in landline phone access showed a dramatic change over the same years as the difference in life evaluation between young and old expanded.
The correlation between landline phone access and life evaluation decreased slightly for the young, r = .16 in 2015-2017 and r = .02 in 2023-2025.
For elders, the correlation decreased from r = .03 in 2015-2017 to -.18 in 2023-2025, reflecting that landline phone access has become a negative marker for elders, among the few people who have it.
In sum, the DID-based model may reflect that what truly explains the increased life evaluation gap between young and old in Norway is unclear in the GWP data.
The few effects were small, and access to landline phones may just reflect a technological development, and may act as a benchmark and face validity of the analysis.

Young adulthood is a formative life stage in which individuals consolidate their identity, complete education, start careers, and establish relationships and families.

Compromised wellbeing during this foundational stage may disrupt these trajectories and carry adverse consequences across the life course (Deighton et al., 2018; Fergusson & Woodward, 2002; McLeod et al., 2016; Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2021).

text.text: Decreasing wellbeing may also signal excess risk of mental health problems, which in turn increase the risk of morbidity (Caspi et al., 2020) and may undermine academic achievement, labor market participation, creativity and innovation, with downstream effects on economic sustainability (Clayborne et al., 2019).
